en: As khan over the lands I had subdued,
While I lived in delight,
Upon my wrist, the all-cutting blade
Hanging there,
Unbelievers and Muslims
While I drove them together,
Why did I not die then?
The lacquered spear of birch wood,
While I bound it fast,
Firing shots across the whole world,
Destroying what I aimed at,
While I waged war,
Why did I not die then?
My companion Manas, would that you had not died!
Would that Bakai had not been left desolate!
Mighty Khan Manas died;
My orphan left by Manas,
My back broken, he too died.
My wings have been bent,
Leaving me sitting in darkness,
My little camel calf, whom I truly mourn,
Bereft of Semetey.
“Sitting here burning with grief,
What wish can I attain?
For the orphan left by Manas,
Let me become a sacrifice.
My lamp, my orphan, would that you had not died!
Would that my head had not suffered humiliation!
I coughed as I herded camels,
Wondering whether my only one would come.
Not granting my wish, O God,
You have laid great sorrow upon my barren head.”
Saying this, Khan Bakai,
Sobbing and lamenting,
A bright dagger with a striped neck
Drew from its sheath.
The lion Bakai, himself
Intending to offer as a sacrifice,
For the sake of his only orphan,
Intending to become a sacrifice.
The warrior Bakai prepared himself
To tear open his ribs;
He meant to end his wretched life,
To shed his own blood.
As he turned Kökcholok's head,
At the root of his fleshly heart,
The bright dagger with its mottled neck,
As he was about to strike with a thud,
As your lion was about to die,
About to see the face of the other world,
Taking his battle-axe, readying himself,
Your orphan left by Manas
“Uncle Bakai, what are you doing?” said,
Pleading with the old man.
The battle-axe in his hand
Semetey seized,
And Khan Bakai's dagger
He struck aside.
Not needing a second blow,
He struck it flying away.
The old wolf-man Bakai
He now saved alive.
“Do not turn your courser's head;
Uncle Bakai, do not cut short your hawk-like life!
You are weeping so much.
What sort of land was your Talas?
What sort of hero was your Manas?
Grieving because the boy has died,
Uncle Bakai, it was God's doing.
The magnanimous lion Manas,
Uncle Bakai, what sort of man did he resemble?
At the age of twelve,
You met Manas.
His figure and bearing,
Did you see them, uncle,
Your wolf-man's appearance when mounted on a horse?”
Upon hearing this, mighty Bakai
Drew back.
Taking a hare's paw in his hand,
He wiped his eyes.
The leopard took a good pinch,
And placed it upon his palate.
Raising his brow, straightening up,
He cast his eyes upon the orphan,
And looked closely at him.
As he observed and looked,
Nose matching nose,
Manas who had passed away,
As though copied from him,
Manas's scalp
Put upon the child again,
As though wrapped about him,
Scalp upon scalp,
As though fitted exactly,
Khan Manas brought back to life,
O God, as though pieced together,
Like the wolf-man Manas himself,
Not the man himself, but like his dark eyes.
Look at the boy's head like a small cauldron;
Look at his brows like a reclining cow.
His eyes were like the beds of lakes,
Like my wolf-man himself.
In the desert of Mediyan,
The wolf-man Manas, the leopard,
Like the place where they had met.
Mighty Bakai gave a sudden start;
Then he knew this was his orphan.
Truly created by God,
He knew him for His servant;
Of his companion, Sultan Manas,
He knew him for the son.
“My shame is covered through him;
What I lost has been found.
Has the orphan I mourned arrived?
Have my eyes seen my orphan?
My exposed flesh has been covered,
My dignity thus restored.
My orphan left by Manas,
To Temir Khan's city,
How you wandered away!
‘The orphan entrusted to us will come,’
How I, Bakai, gazed in longing!
To Bukhara with its city,
How you fled away!
‘My support, my orphan, will come,’
Without dying or perishing, upon the plain,
How I herded camels!
My spring flowing from the hills,
My little one left by magnanimous Manas!”
Howling and wailing, Bakai's
Voice reached God.
The skillful leopard Bakai,
The orphan from horseback
Snatched up and fell to the earth.
He opened his mouth wide as a maw,
Pressed Semetey to his breast.
For the time it takes to cook meat, mighty Bakai
Lay there shaking with sobs.
As Bakai pressed him to his breast,
At that moment Semetey,
Inside and out turned to embers,
Burned brightly,
His skin seething like fire.
The old man Bakai,
Shaking, would not let him go.
If you looked at his whole body,
It trembled like lead.
Opening their arms wide,
Satisfying their longing fully,
Elder and younger greeting one another,
Then kissing without restraint.
Mighty Bakai was overcome.
“Am I awake or dreaming?
Has the orphan truly come?
Is it truly my own orphan?”
Bakai hugged him firmly,
Crying out with all his heart.
Khan Bakai wept greatly;
Semetey too wept.
Thus sharing their hearts,
O wonder, father and son met.
Doing all these things,
Father and son found one another.
The precious leopard Bakai,
Hugging him again and again,
His thoughts scattered in many directions,
Would not let the boy go.
Semetey, at his wits' end,
His father's Boz Kise belt
Slung about his neck:
“May I be your sacrifice, dear uncle,
My ribs are cracking apart!
Let me go, uncle, let me go!
My soul cries out within my breast;
Inside and out I am on fire,
Uncle, I am burning, aching sorely.
Uncle, do not send me off before my time,
Do not kill me before I die!”
When his uncle Bakai heard this,
He gathered his wits at once;
Khan Bakai released
The boy within his arms.
“God has granted my wish,” he said,
“The orphan I awaited has arrived.”
What was broken in me was joined,
And thus my soul rejoiced.
He cried “Baabedin!” at once,
And vowed a sheep to Koroshon.
To Almighty God above
He vowed a mare with moon-white hooves.
To generous Manas's spirit,
Where he named the vow, he pledged a camel.
His orphan had arrived, grown up;
Thus Bakai rejoined his people's ranks.
When he lay down, sleep would not come;
Once that boy had arrived,
His old age no longer showed.
As though he had turned fifteen,
Mighty Bakai came into the light;
His story brings the soul to grief—
Mighty Bakai found his speech.
When leopard Manas died back then,
The white tiger that had fled
Was now beside Sultan Bakai,
The leopard, bounding at his flank.
The forty chiltens and Khizr Ilyas
Readied themselves on Bakai's forty sides.
When he turned to face the foe,
While tiger Manas still was there,
Tiger Bakai, the leopard,
In the days God favored him—
Khan Bakai's blue-gray bull
Had fled away before;
Since Bakai had last seen that bull,
Twelve years had passed for him.
The blue-gray bull with short, thick horns
Bounded and charged across his path.
Old tiger Bakai's
Lost guardians were found again.
Tiger Bakai, the elder,
If deeds lay six months away,
Was a saint who knew them now,
A true servant loved by God,
My uncle Bakai, Oluyat's own son.
The Pleiades are the sign of dawn;
He was Khan Manas's companion,
Who found the right word in surprise,
Who found his sight in darkness.
Placed in front, he brought good fortune;
Bakai behind was like a host of troops.
Then orphan Semetey looked:
Once his guardians had returned,
Once God had granted him his wish,
At one glance Bakai was one man;
My word, at another, a thousand men!
When he turned his front toward you,
My word, he had a dragon's form.
When my uncle turned his back,
He bore the awe of six thousand heroes.
For my fierce father Manas,
Bakai was an unbreakable iron fort.
My father, leopard Manas,
Had found a lion equal to him.
My dear mother Kanykei—
The poor woman's words were true.
This fierce father of mine, Manas,
He had planted and raised into a garden,
And built and raised into a house.
He laid low the foes they faced,
And made my valiant father khan.
What had broken for my father,
He truly joined together;
What had scattered for my father—
He truly gathered up.
He entered Beijing and attacked,
And truly opened up the road.
